name: Executive Order of November 9, 1855 setting apart the Coast (later Siletz) Reservation, as mapped on Royce areas 578 and 579
aka: Alsea and Siletz reservations (Royce areas 578 and 579)
citation: Executive Order of November 9, 1855 (Royce schedule p. 814); Royce maps the reservation through its later reductions, areas 578, 579 and 479 (p. 815)
nations: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians (Tillamook, Alsea, Yaquina, Coos, Lower Umpqua, Siuslaw, Tututni, Coquille, Chetco and other peoples placed on the Coast Reservation)
promises: Not a treaty: a presidential order. It set apart the Coast Reservation for the Indians on the coast of Oregon, from the mouth of the Tsiltcoos River north to a point due east of Cape Lookout (Royce, p. 814).

Royce gives the order no area number of its own; its map column reads See 578, 579, 479 (p. 815). Areas 578 and 579 are the parts that the Act of March 3, 1875 threw open to settlement (578) and kept as a permanent reservation (579) (Royce, p. 878).

Its boundaries were almost identical with the reservation promised in the unratified coast treaty of 1855, and it was created subject to future diminution (United States v. Alcea Band of Tillamooks, 1946).

breaches.what: The Supreme Court affirmed a Court of Claims judgment that the Tillamook, Coquille, Tututni and Chetco lost their original Indian title through this order without consent or compensation, the Court of Claims finding the taking complete on November 9, 1855, and held they were entitled to compensation under the jurisdictional act of 1935. A large part of the reservation was Tillamook land.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States v. Alcea Band of Tillamooks, 329 U.S. 40 (1946), affirming Alcea Band of Tillamooks v. United States, 103 Ct. Cl. 494 (1945)

source.title: United States v. Alcea Band of Tillamooks, 329 U.S. 40 (1946)
source.publisher: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School

breaches.quote: were deprived of their original possessions by the Executive Order of November 9, 1855

breaches.what: The Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians say the reservation was created under their ratified western Oregon treaties, not as a temporary measure, and that the false account of it as temporary was used to open most of their lands to settlement without treaty agreement or compensation and to force the 1892 cession.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians, Creating the Coast (Siletz) Reservation

landTaken: Alcea (1946) treats the order itself as the taking of the four tribes’ original Indian title, and says a large part of the reservation was Tillamook land. The Indian Claims Commission later said the Siletz land ceded in 1892, which lies in area 579, is part of the land in the Alcea case (Docket 239 opinion, 1955). No acreage for the 1855 taking was found.
compensation: Alcea (1946) held the four tribes entitled to compensation under the Act of August 26, 1935. The Docket 239 opinion (1955) notes the Court of Claims valued the Alcea lands as of 1855 at $1.20 an acre (115 Ct. Cl. 463, 1950). The amount recovered was not recorded in this pass.
today: In 1875 Congress approved the 1855 and 1865 orders and removed more land from the reservation to open it for settlement (Alcea, 1946); Royce maps the land thrown open as area 578 and the tract kept as a permanent reservation as area 579. That Act is the separate record cession-1875-03-03-indians-on-the-oregon-coast. Area 579 lost its unallotted land under the 1892 agreement ratified August 15, 1894, a price the Indian Claims Commission found unconscionable in Docket 239 (cession-1894-08-15-indians-on-coast-of-oregon). The same 1855 order as mapped on area 479 is cession-1855-11-09-indians-on-coast-of-oregon.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says its reservation was a permanent reservation under its ratified treaties, and that calling it temporary was a misreading later used to take most of it.
The Tribe says the 1875 Act opened about 700,000 more acres to non-Indians on a false report that the Yachats headmen had consented, leaving about 225,000 acres.

openQuestions: treaties.json gives this entry and cession-1875-03-03-indians-on-the-oregon-coast the same Royce areas (578, 579) and the same statute links. This entry is dated and named for the 1855 order (Royce p. 814), and the 1855 order is also the separate entry cession-1855-11-09-indians-on-coast-of-oregon (area 479). Not edited.

Whether the land of areas 578 and 579 lay within Tillamook, Alsea or other original title was not mapped; Alcea speaks of the four claimant tribes only. The Alsea, Siuslaw, Coos and Lower Umpqua were not parties to Alcea.
The amount the Alcea tribes finally recovered was not traced.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 12): the file was rewritten to rest on the 1855 order itself. It had been researched as the Act of March 3, 1875 (its act-of-congress and nation-statement breaches were both about that Act), which is the separate record cession-1875-03-03-indians-on-the-oregon-coast; keeping them here would count one Act twice. The 1875 Act now appears only in today and nationVoice. Status stays broken on the Alcea ruling, which concerns the 1855 order and, per the Docket 239 opinion, land inside area 579.
2026-11-08: counted once with cession-1855-11-09-indians-on-coast-of-oregon (the same 1855 Coast Reservation order, listed twice). The map still shows this row.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: an 1855 presidential order setting apart the Coast Reservation for the Indians of the Oregon coast. It was made subject to later reduction.
plain.happened: The Supreme Court upheld in 1946 a ruling that the Tillamook, Coquille, Tututni and Chetco lost their original title through this order without consent or compensation. The Siletz Tribe says the reservation was permanent and later wrongly treated as temporary.
plain.today: The four tribes were held entitled to compensation; the amount has not been traced. Congress cut the reservation in 1875, and its unallotted land was ceded in 1892 for a price later found unconscionable.
